title: Western Wei
capsule: Western Wei (西魏, 535–557) was one of the two successor regimes of the fragmented Northern Wei, controlling the Wei River valley, the Guanzhong plain, and parts of Sichuan from its capital Chang'an, while the rival Eastern Wei held the North China Plain at Ye. Real power resided not with the nominal Tuoba Xianbei emperors but with the generalissimo Yuwen Tai, who restructured the army around the fubing militia system and decisively defeated the Eastern Wei at the Battle of Shayuan in 537; in 551 he also cemented a marriage alliance with the Göktürk leader Bumin Qaghan. Yuwen Tai died in 556, and the following year his nephew Yuwen Jue deposed the last Western Wei emperor Yuan Kuo and proclaimed the Northern Zhou dynasty, inheriting the same fubing institution later adopted by the Sui and Tang.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core territory around the Guanzhong basin is well attested by Chinese annalistic sources; frontier lines with Eastern Wei and the southern Liang dynasty fluctuated and are approximated.
